extracted.intended_audience: media/journalism scholars, students and researchers studying news values, news discourse and press photography
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing news values in news discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, categorising and applying news values and photo-specific news factors used as selection criteria in journalism studies and news production. Includes linguistic and semiotic resources that construct newsworthiness in print and photographic news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed by Brighton & Foy (2007) as one of their 'new news values'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of an updated set of news values intended to reflect a cultural shift in provider/consumer relations; treated as a selection criterion applied to prioritize items (Brighton & Foy 2007: 25-29).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Named by Brighton & Foy (2007) as a new news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a selection criterion for prioritising items in the digital/converged media age (Brighton & Foy 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Included in Brighton & Foy's list of new news values and also used by Bell to mean the mix of similar/different kinds of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers both to content-mix considerations in editorial selection and to formal/compositional aspects; treated as a factor that can influence whether a story is selected/placed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Brighton & Foy's 'new news values'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of their catalogue of selection criteria intended to account for contemporary news culture and liveness in broadcast media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: Named by Brighton & Foy; aligns with traditional values like Novelty/Unexpectedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals that events deviating from the ordinary are prioritized; appears across multiple authors as a core newsworthiness attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed by Brighton & Foy as a news value (called 'Worth' in their list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture perceived importance or significance of an event when editors decide to prioritize coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: External influences (External Factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brighton & Foy (2007) add 'External influences' to capture pressures from outside the industry (e.g. proprietor, advertiser, politician).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats outside pressure as an explicit news value/factor that can corrupt or shape selection and treatment of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture opportunities (sub-category of Entertainment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harcup & O'Neill identify a sub-category of the news value 'entertainment' labelled 'picture opportunities' (p. 274).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story provides a good picture opportunity it was often included even when there was little intrinsic newsworthiness; combined with celebrity, sex, animals etc. this can 'guarantee' coverage (examples and quote from Harcup & O'Neill 2001: 274, 276).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization / availability of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Presented as a selection criterion in studies of press photography (e.g. Rössler et al. 2011; Harcup & O'Neill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence or accessibility of images (or the potential to visualize an event) can determine whether stories are published or given priority; images may perform functions distinct from accompanying text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite persons / Prominence / Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Craig (1994) lists 'reference to elite persons'; Cotter and others discuss 'Prominence' as a news value about the standing of actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elite status or prominence of actors increases newsworthiness; examples include coverage bias toward A-list celebrities or high-status individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Craig (1994) detects 'personalization' as a news value in press photographs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on individuals (rather than abstract processes) increases perceived newsworthiness; linguistic devices and framing can construct personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as a news value in Craig (1994) and elsewhere (Bell/van Dijk reference to negativity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative events or interpretations (e.g. conflict, harm) are privileged as newsworthy; appears as both a cognitive constraint and a content value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict / Dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Craig (1994) identifies 'conflict/dramatization' as a value in press photographs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories or images emphasizing conflict or dramatic elements are more likely to be selected; combined with good pictures/celebrities this is a 'heady brew' for editors (Harcup & O'Neill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Rössler et al.'s (2011) 'image-inherent news factors' used to judge whether images are 'worth publishing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photo news factor indicating visible physical or material harm in an image; used as an empirical selection factor in studies of press photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence / Aggression
rubrics_metrics.description: Rössler et al. (2011) list violence/aggression as a photo news factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of violent/aggressive content in photographs increases likelihood of publication and audience impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Included in Rössler et al.'s catalogue of photo news factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images that imply or show contentious, contested or scandalous elements are more publishable and newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrities
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as a photo news factor (Rössler et al.) and repeatedly cited (Harcup & O'Neill) as guaranteeing coverage when combined with picture opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to well-known public figures makes stories/photos more newsworthy; often interacts with other values (picture, sex, TV, animals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Term appears across multiple lists (Rössler, Bell, Brighton & Foy) as a core news value (also termed Novelty or Unusualness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events or images that deviate from expectation increase newsworthiness; linguistic markers like 'reveal' or 'disclose' can enhance this value (Bednarek examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rössler et al. include 'emotions' as an image-inherent news factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs that display or evoke emotions are judged more publishable and impactful; emotional content contributes to perceived newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Rössler et al.'s photo news factors (labelled 'execution and technique').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographic quality, composition and technical execution influence selection and assessment of images for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality / Eroticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Included by Rössler et al. as a photo news factor that makes images more publishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual or erotic content in images can increase newsworthiness or editorial interest, though ethical/legal norms may moderate usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency / Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell lists Recency; Singletary & Lamb cite timeliness as a yardstick for award-winning press photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent events are privileged; temporal proximity to the occurrence increases selection probability (a core classical news value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell identifies 'Superlativeness' as a content news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme, record-breaking or superlative aspects of events make them more newsworthy and likely to be emphasized in copy-editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell lists 'Continuity' as a news-gathering/processing value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing stories or developments are privileged for follow-up coverage and placement decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell's news-gathering/processing value 'Competition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition between outlets and the drive to scoop influences selection decisions and can shape how news values are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell includes 'Prefabrication' as a news-gathering/processing value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-arranged or anticipated stories (religious holidays, scheduled events) have built-in news value and influence newsroom planning and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell names 'Clarity' as one of three values concerning quality/style of news text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear writing is an objective of news text and copy-editing; clarity is treated as a goal that enhances news value in presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell lists 'Brevity' as a text-quality news value/goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness in news writing/editing is a quality criterion and serves to maximise perceived news value and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell includes 'Colour' (vivacity, human-interest detail) as a text-quality value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of vivid detail, human-interest elements, and engaging language enhances the engagingness and perceived newsworthiness of copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Dijk lists 'Novelty' among specific cognitive constraints that define news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newness or previously unknown aspects contribute to cognitive representation of newsworthiness and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presupposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Dijk identifies 'Presupposition' as a cognitive constraint/news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background assumptions and what is taken for granted can shape how events are interpreted as newsworthy in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Dijk names 'Consonance' as a news value (events that fit existing narratives/codes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that fit established narrative codes or expectations are more readily interpreted and selected as news (Bignell's related point about narrative codes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance and Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Dijk groups 'Deviance and Negativity' among cognitive constraints defining news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviation from norms and explicitly negative aspects are cognitively salient and therefore more likely to be selected and foregrounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Named by van Dijk and Singletary & Lamb as an important news value (physical/social closeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic, cultural or social closeness of events/actors to the audience increases perceived relevance and selection likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Singletary & Lamb find human interest as a news value for feature photos (and in other literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories/images that foreground human-interest elements (emotion, personalization) are often prioritized in features and some news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximizing/enhancing news value through language and editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell and others argue that journalists and copy-editors can 'enhance' or 'maximize' news value via language choices and editing (e.g. use of reveal, revelation, evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: copy-editing aims to maximise news value; lexical choices (reveal/disclose) enhance Unexpectedness; evaluations can construct Prominence or Eliteness; journalists may deliberately select phrasing to foreground particular news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic and semiotic devices as constructors of newsworthiness (discursive approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bednarek & Caple's discursive approach: news values are discursively constructed and newsworthiness becomes a quality of texts; semiotic devices (language, photos, layout, typography) construct newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic focus is on cataloguing the semiotic resources that construct news values across phases of the news process (published stories, input material, newsroom talk). The approach treats news values as qualities constructed through discourse and multimodal resources rather than solely pre-existing external criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic sign / formal photographic news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Hall (1973) describes a 'formal news value of the photographic sign' (e.g. the elaboration of the photograph and text in professional ideology terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal photographic news values include the unexpected, dramatic, recent event concerning a person of high status; there is also an ideological level of connoted themes and interpretations that images may carry.
